The book of Judges ended with a refrain that hung in the air like an unanswered question: in those days there was no king in Israel. The book of ⟦p:ruth_2450|Ruth⟧ ended with a name, ⟦p:david_994|David⟧, the great-grandson of a Moabite widow and a farmer from ⟦l:bethlehem_218|Bethlehem⟧. First ⟦p:samuel_2469|Samuel⟧ brings those two threads together. It tells how Israel moved from the loose federation of tribes we have seen under the judges to a kingdom with a crown, and how the crown passed, by a long and painful road, from the first king to the man God had chosen.

First and Second ⟦p:samuel_2469|Samuel⟧ were originally one book in the Hebrew Bible. They were divided later, when the Scriptures were translated into Greek and the long scroll was split in two. The book is named after Samuel, its great figure in the early chapters, and his death is recorded well before the story of First Samuel is over. Later Scripture says that the acts of ⟦p:david_994|David⟧ were written in the records of Samuel the seer, Nathan the prophet and Gad the seer, and Jewish tradition holds that these three men gave us this book.

The events belong to the eleventh century before Christ. Israel's tribes are settled in the hill country on both sides of the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧, but they are under growing pressure. The Philistines, whom we met in the days of ⟦p:samson_2468|Samson⟧, now dominate the coastal plain from their five cities and push steadily into the hills. They are well organised, well armed, and they control the working of iron. Israel has no army beyond whatever the tribes can muster, and its leadership has grown weak. At ⟦l:shiloh_1081|Shiloh⟧, where the tabernacle stands, the old priest ⟦p:eli_1072|Eli⟧ presides, but his sons, who serve as priests, are corrupt.

Three lives dominate the book. The first is ⟦p:samuel_2469|Samuel⟧ himself. He is born in answer to a mother's prayer, given to the Lord as a small child, and raised at ⟦l:shiloh_1081|Shiloh⟧. He becomes a prophet, offers sacrifice at Israel's altars, and is the last of the judges. Samuel is a bridge between two eras. He is the one who warns Israel what a king will cost them, and he is the one who anoints, first, ⟦p:saul_2478|Saul⟧, and then ⟦p:david_994|David⟧.

The second is ⟦p:saul_2478|Saul⟧, a tall and impressive young man from the tribe of ⟦p:benjamin_463|Benjamin⟧, from the town of ⟦l:gibeah_466|Gibeah⟧. His early days as king are full of promise. But Saul is a troubled figure, impatient, insecure and unwilling to obey, and the book traces his decline with something close to tragedy: his rejection by God, his loss of ⟦p:holy_spirit_7400|the Spirit⟧, his jealous rage, and finally his despair.

The third is ⟦p:david_994|David⟧, the youngest son of ⟦p:jesse_903|Jesse⟧ of ⟦l:bethlehem_218|Bethlehem⟧, a shepherd boy anointed in his father's house while ⟦p:saul_2478|Saul⟧ still reigns. He enters Saul's court as a musician to soothe the king, steps into the open as the champion who faces the Philistine giant ⟦p:goliath_1327|Goliath⟧, and becomes Saul's most successful commander, the close friend of Saul's son ⟦p:jonathan_1692|Jonathan⟧ and the husband of his daughter ⟦p:michal_2073|Michal⟧. Then Saul turns against him, and for the second half of the book David lives as a fugitive, hiding in the wilderness of Judah, gathering a band of outcasts, even taking refuge among the Philistines. Twice he has the chance to kill Saul, and twice he refuses to lift his hand against the Lord's anointed.

Behind these lives the book raises the question of what kind of king Israel should have. The people's demand for a king, so that they can be like the other nations, is treated as a rejection of God's own rule. Yet God gives them a king, and kingship itself becomes part of his purpose. The difference lies in the heart of the man who holds the throne. That is the contrast the book draws between ⟦p:saul_2478|Saul⟧ and ⟦p:david_994|David⟧, though it is honest about David's failings too, and his gravest ones still lie ahead.

The book also has its moments of tenderness and surprise: ⟦p:hannah_1400|Hannah⟧'s song of praise, the boy ⟦p:samuel_2469|Samuel⟧ hearing his name called in the night, the ark of God captured by the Philistines and sent back, the friendship of ⟦p:david_994|David⟧ and ⟦p:jonathan_1692|Jonathan⟧, and the wise intervention of a woman named ⟦p:abigail_26|Abigail⟧. Its final scenes are dark. Samuel dies. ⟦p:saul_2478|Saul⟧, abandoned and afraid before a last battle with the Philistines, seeks out a medium at Endor. The book ends on the slopes of ⟦l:mount_gilboa_837|Mount Gilboa⟧, with the king and his sons dead and the Philistines victorious. Second Samuel will open with David hearing the news.

The book begins, as several great stories in the Bible begin, with a woman who cannot have children. Her name is ⟦p:hannah_1400|Hannah⟧, and she is one of the two wives of a man named ⟦p:elkanah_1168|Elkanah⟧, from ⟦l:ramathaim-zophim_977|Ramathaim-zophim⟧, usually shortened to ⟦l:ramah_975|Ramah⟧, in the hill country of ⟦p:ephraim_1206|Ephraim⟧. His other wife, ⟦p:peninnah_2313|Peninnah⟧, has children, and she uses that to torment Hannah year after year.

Every year the family goes up to ⟦l:shiloh_1081|Shiloh⟧ to worship and offer sacrifice at the tabernacle. This is still the time of the judges, and Shiloh is still Israel's central sanctuary. The old priest there is ⟦p:eli_1072|Eli⟧, and his two sons, ⟦p:hophni_1550|Hophni⟧ and ⟦p:phinehas_2350|Phinehas⟧, also serve as priests. The listener is told their names in the opening verses, because they will matter.

⟦p:elkanah_1168|Elkanah⟧ loves ⟦p:hannah_1400|Hannah⟧ and gives her a double portion, and he asks her gently whether he is not better to her than ten sons. One year at ⟦l:shiloh_1081|Shiloh⟧, after the sacrificial meal, Hannah goes to the sanctuary to pray, weeping, while ⟦p:eli_1072|Eli⟧ sits watching by the doorpost. Her prayer includes a vow that echoes the story of ⟦p:samson_2468|Samson⟧: if God gives her a son, no razor will touch his head, and the boy will belong to the Lord for life. 2:
⟦p:hannah_1400|Hannah⟧ has kept her vow. Once her son ⟦p:samuel_2469|Samuel⟧ was weaned, she brought him to ⟦l:shiloh_1081|Shiloh⟧ and gave him to the Lord's service, under the care of ⟦p:eli_1072|Eli⟧. Now she prays again, but this time with joy.

Her prayer is a song that reaches far beyond her own story. It celebrates a God who turns the world upside down, who breaks the bows of the mighty, feeds the hungry, lifts the poor from the dust and gives children to the barren. It ends with a word that is surprising in a book that opens without a king: the Lord will give strength to his king and exalt the horn of his anointed. Many centuries later Mary's song in the Gospel of ⟦p:luke_1836|Luke⟧ would echo ⟦p:hannah_1400|Hannah⟧'s.

The chapter then alternates between two pictures. On one side are ⟦p:eli_1072|Eli⟧'s sons, ⟦p:hophni_1550|Hophni⟧ and ⟦p:phinehas_2350|Phinehas⟧, who treat the sacrifices with contempt, take the best meat by force, and sleep with the women who serve at the entrance to the tabernacle. On the other is the boy ⟦p:samuel_2469|Samuel⟧, ministering before the Lord in a small linen ephod, with a new robe each year from his mother. Eli rebukes his sons, but too mildly and too late. 3:
The boy ⟦p:samuel_2469|Samuel⟧ is growing up at ⟦l:shiloh_1081|Shiloh⟧, serving before the Lord under the old priest ⟦p:eli_1072|Eli⟧. The chapter opens with a sentence that describes the whole era: in those days the word of the Lord was rare, and visions were few. Eli's eyes have grown so dim that he can no longer see. It is night, and Samuel is lying down in the sanctuary, where the ark of God is kept, before the lamp of God has gone out.

Then the Lord calls the boy by name. ⟦p:samuel_2469|Samuel⟧ does not yet know the Lord's voice, because the Lord has not yet spoken to him, and the scene that follows is told with gentle repetition. Each time he runs to ⟦p:eli_1072|Eli⟧. At the third call it is the old priest who understands what is happening and tells the boy how to answer.

The first message ⟦p:samuel_2469|Samuel⟧ receives is a hard one, a confirmation of the judgement already spoken against ⟦p:eli_1072|Eli⟧'s household. In the morning Samuel is afraid to tell him. Eli's response, when the boy finally tells him everything, is one of quiet resignation. By the close, Samuel is recognised throughout Israel, from ⟦p:dan_973|Dan⟧ to ⟦l:beersheba_170|Beersheba⟧, as a prophet of the Lord. The silence of heaven has been broken.
4:
⟦p:samuel_2469|Samuel⟧'s word is now heard throughout Israel, but the next scene leaves him offstage entirely. War breaks out with the Philistines. Israel camps at a place called ⟦l:ebenezer_350|Ebenezer⟧, and the Philistines at ⟦l:aphek_72|Aphek⟧, on the edge of the coastal plain, near the route that led up into the hill country. The first battle goes badly, and Israel loses about four thousand men.

The elders' response reveals how far Israel has drifted. Rather than seeking the Lord, they send to ⟦l:shiloh_1081|Shiloh⟧ for the ark of the covenant, as though it were a charm that could guarantee victory. The ark had once gone before Israel across the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧ and around ⟦l:jericho_634|Jericho⟧, but now it is sent for like a weapon, with no word from the God whose presence it represented. ⟦p:eli_1072|Eli⟧'s two sons, ⟦p:hophni_1550|Hophni⟧ and ⟦p:phinehas_2350|Phinehas⟧, come with it into the camp, and the great shout that greets it terrifies the Philistines, who have heard of the God who struck ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧.

The judgement spoken against ⟦p:eli_1072|Eli⟧'s house is about to fall. The second half of the chapter moves back to ⟦l:shiloh_1081|Shiloh⟧, where Eli, ninety-eight years old and blind, sits by the road watching, his heart trembling for the ark, waiting for news. 5:
The ark of the covenant has been captured. ⟦p:eli_1072|Eli⟧ and both his sons are dead, and ⟦p:phinehas_2350|Phinehas⟧'s widow has died giving birth to a son she named ⟦p:ichabod_1589|Ichabod⟧, meaning the glory has departed. In Israel it seems that God himself has been defeated.

The Philistines certainly think so. They carry the ark from the battlefield to ⟦l:ashdod_101|Ashdod⟧, one of their five chief cities, near the coast, and set it in the temple of their god ⟦p:dagon_969|Dagon⟧, beside his statue. In the ancient world this was what victors did with the gods of a conquered people: they placed them as trophies before their own god, as a sign of who was stronger.

But this chapter is about the God of Israel acting alone, without priests, without an army, and in enemy territory. The story is told with grim humour. ⟦p:dagon_969|Dagon⟧'s statue is found face down before the ark, as if bowing. Then a plague breaks out among the people of ⟦l:ashdod_101|Ashdod⟧. The Philistine rulers send the ark on to ⟦l:gath_442|Gath⟧, and then on to ⟦l:ekron_364|Ekron⟧, and the same thing happens in each city. The capture that seemed to prove Israel's God powerless has become a disaster for his captors.
6:
The ark has been in Philistine territory for seven months, passed from city to city, leaving plague behind it. The Philistine leaders now want only to be rid of it, and they ask their priests and diviners how to send it home safely.

The advice they receive is careful and, in its own way, respectful. The ark must not go back empty. It must be sent with a guilt offering, gold images of the tumours and of the rats that have ravaged the land, one for each of the five Philistine cities. The priests even recall what happened to ⟦p:pharaoh_2331|Pharaoh⟧ when he hardened his heart. And they devise a test. Two milk cows that have never been yoked will pull the cart, while their calves are penned up at home. If the cows leave their calves and go straight up the road toward Israel, the disaster came from Israel's God. If not, it was chance.

The road leads east into the Sorek Valley, the same valley where ⟦p:samson_2468|Samson⟧ once met ⟦p:delilah_1005|Delilah⟧, toward ⟦l:beth-shemesh_234|Beth-shemesh⟧, an Israelite town where the people are harvesting wheat. The ark has come to rest at ⟦l:kiriath-jearim_701|Kiriath-jearim⟧, a hill town on the border between Judah and ⟦p:benjamin_463|Benjamin⟧, in the house of a man named ⟦p:abinadab_43|Abinadab⟧, whose son ⟦p:eleazar_1062|Eleazar⟧ is set apart to guard it. ⟦p:samuel_2469|Samuel⟧ has been absent from the story since the battle at ⟦l:aphek_72|Aphek⟧. Now he steps forward again, as a grown man and Israel's leader. His message is direct: if you are truly returning to the Lord, put away the foreign gods and the Ashtoreths, and serve him only. The outcome is the reverse of the disaster at ⟦l:aphek_72|Aphek⟧, and Samuel marks the victory with a stone, which he names ⟦l:ebenezer_350|Ebenezer⟧, the stone of help. A brief summary then sketches Samuel's long years of leadership as a judge, travelling on a yearly circuit from ⟦l:bethel_202|Bethel⟧ to ⟦l:gilgal_476|Gilgal⟧ to ⟦l:mizpah_811|Mizpah⟧, and home to ⟦l:ramah_975|Ramah⟧.
8:
Years have passed. ⟦p:samuel_2469|Samuel⟧ is old, and he has made his sons, ⟦p:joel_1647|Joel⟧ and ⟦p:abiah_15|Abijah⟧, judges in ⟦l:beersheba_170|Beersheba⟧, in the far south. But they take bribes and pervert justice, just as ⟦p:eli_1072|Eli⟧'s sons once abused the priesthood. Israel's leadership is failing again, from within.

So the elders of Israel come to ⟦p:samuel_2469|Samuel⟧ at ⟦l:ramah_975|Ramah⟧ with a request that changes the course of their history. Appoint a king to judge us, they say, like all the other nations. Their reasons are understandable. Samuel is ageing, his sons are corrupt, and as later chapters make clear, enemies are pressing on every side. ⟦p:samuel_2469|Samuel⟧ is deeply displeased, and he takes the matter to the Lord. God's answer is that the people have not rejected Samuel but God himself, as their king. Yet he tells Samuel to give them what they ask, and to warn them first. What follows is Samuel's description of the ways of a king, built around a single, repeated verb: he will take. The people listen, and they insist.
9:
The people have asked for a king, and the Lord has told ⟦p:samuel_2469|Samuel⟧ to give them one. Now the story moves, without warning, to a different family and a very ordinary errand. ⟦p:kish_1784|Kish⟧, a man of standing in the tribe of ⟦p:benjamin_463|Benjamin⟧, has lost some donkeys, and he sends his son ⟦p:saul_2478|Saul⟧, with a servant, to find them.

⟦p:saul_2478|Saul⟧ is introduced as choice and handsome, a head taller than anyone else in Israel. He looks every inch a king. The search takes them through the hill country of ⟦p:ephraim_1206|Ephraim⟧ and the land of ⟦p:benjamin_463|Benjamin⟧ for three days, until they reach the district of Zuph and Saul is ready to give up. The listener knows more than ⟦p:saul_2478|Saul⟧ does. When Saul and Samuel meet at the town gate, Saul has no idea who he is talking to. By evening he has been given the place of honour at a sacrificial meal and spoken with privately on Samuel's roof. 10:
At the edge of the town, with the servant out of earshot, ⟦p:samuel_2469|Samuel⟧ takes a flask of oil and pours it on ⟦p:saul_2478|Saul⟧'s head. Anointing with oil set a person apart for a sacred task, as Israel's priests had been set apart in the wilderness. Now it marks Israel's first king.

To confirm that this is truly from God, ⟦p:samuel_2469|Samuel⟧ gives ⟦p:saul_2478|Saul⟧ three signs that will happen on his way home: news of the donkeys at ⟦p:rachel_2386|Rachel⟧'s tomb, a meeting with three men going up to worship at ⟦l:bethel_202|Bethel⟧, and an encounter with a band of prophets near ⟦l:gibeah_466|Gibeah⟧, where ⟦p:holy_spirit_7400|the Spirit⟧ of the Lord will come upon him. The second half of the chapter makes the private anointing public. ⟦p:samuel_2469|Samuel⟧ gathers the tribes at ⟦l:mizpah_811|Mizpah⟧ and, after rebuking them once more for rejecting God as their king, has lots cast before the Lord, tribe by tribe and clan by clan, to reveal the man God has chosen. But when ⟦p:saul_2478|Saul⟧'s name comes up, he cannot be found. He has hidden among the baggage. 11:
⟦p:saul_2478|Saul⟧ has been proclaimed king at ⟦l:mizpah_811|Mizpah⟧, but he has returned home to ⟦l:gibeah_466|Gibeah⟧ and gone back to farming. Israel has a king in name, but he has not yet done anything. Then a crisis comes from across the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧.

⟦p:nahash_2136|Nahash⟧, king of the ⟦l:ammon_58|Ammonites⟧, lays siege to ⟦l:jabesh-gilead_611|Jabesh-gilead⟧, an Israelite town in the hills of ⟦l:gilead_475|Gilead⟧ east of the river. The listener may remember Jabesh-gilead from the end of Judges, when its people were punished for failing to join the war against ⟦p:benjamin_463|Benjamin⟧, and four hundred of its young women were given as wives to the surviving Benjamites. There are old ties between this town and ⟦p:saul_2478|Saul⟧'s tribe.

⟦p:nahash_2136|Nahash⟧'s terms of surrender are brutal: he will gouge out the right eye of every man, as a humiliation to all Israel. The elders of ⟦l:jabesh_610|Jabesh⟧ ask for seven days to seek help. When the messengers reach ⟦l:gibeah_466|Gibeah⟧, ⟦p:saul_2478|Saul⟧ is coming in from the field behind his oxen. What happens next is the moment Saul becomes a king in fact as well as name. His response echoes, in a striking way, the summons the Levite sent to the tribes in the days of the judges, and it rouses the whole nation.
12:
⟦p:saul_2478|Saul⟧ has rescued ⟦l:jabesh-gilead_611|Jabesh-gilead⟧, and at ⟦l:gilgal_476|Gilgal⟧ the people have confirmed him as king amid great rejoicing. Now ⟦p:samuel_2469|Samuel⟧ addresses the assembly. It is a kind of farewell, not to life, for Samuel will live on for some years yet, but to the role he has held as Israel's judge. The leadership now passes to the king.

⟦p:samuel_2469|Samuel⟧ begins by asking the people to testify to his own integrity. Has he taken anyone's ox or donkey, cheated anyone, or accepted a bribe? It is a pointed question after his warning that a king would take. Then he reviews Israel's history since ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧, the pattern familiar from Judges, of forgetting the Lord, oppression, crying out and deliverance. He reminds them that when ⟦p:nahash_2136|Nahash⟧ threatened them, they demanded a king, even though the Lord was their king.

To underline his words, ⟦p:samuel_2469|Samuel⟧ calls on the Lord to send thunder and rain. It is the wheat harvest, early in the summer, a season when rain in that land is rare. The people are terrified, and they ask Samuel to pray for them. His answer combines warning with reassurance, and with a promise that he will not stop praying for them.
13:
⟦p:saul_2478|Saul⟧ is king, and the war with the Philistines that has shadowed the whole story now begins in earnest. He sends most of the people home and keeps three thousand men under arms, two thousand with himself and a thousand with his son.

That son is a new character, introduced without explanation: ⟦p:jonathan_1692|Jonathan⟧, already old enough to command a thousand men. The setting is the hill country of ⟦p:benjamin_463|Benjamin⟧ a few miles north of ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, where ⟦l:geba_447|Geba⟧ and ⟦l:michmash_793|Michmash⟧ face each other across a deep ravine. Jonathan attacks a Philistine outpost at Geba, and the Philistines respond in overwhelming force, with chariots, horsemen and troops like the sand on the seashore. Many Israelites hide in caves and cisterns, and some flee across the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧.

⟦p:saul_2478|Saul⟧ waits at ⟦l:gilgal_476|Gilgal⟧, as ⟦p:samuel_2469|Samuel⟧ told him, for seven days. His army is melting away, and Samuel has not come. What Saul does next seems understandable, even prudent, and it costs him dearly. Samuel's verdict introduces, for the first time, the idea of another man, a man after God's own heart. A striking detail closes the chapter: the Philistines control the work of the blacksmith, so that only Saul and ⟦p:jonathan_1692|Jonathan⟧ have swords or spears.
14:
The Philistines are camped at ⟦l:michmash_793|Michmash⟧, and ⟦p:saul_2478|Saul⟧ sits under a pomegranate tree on the edge of ⟦l:gibeah_466|Gibeah⟧ with about six hundred men. With him is a priest named Ahijah, a great-grandson of ⟦p:eli_1072|Eli⟧, wearing the ephod used to seek God's guidance.

⟦p:jonathan_1692|Jonathan⟧, ⟦p:saul_2478|Saul⟧'s son, does not wait. Without telling his father, he and his armour-bearer set out to cross the ravine between Geba and ⟦l:michmash_793|Michmash⟧, a steep gorge with rocky cliffs on either side, to the Philistine outpost on the far side. His words to the young man reveal his faith: nothing can stop the Lord from saving, whether by many or by few. The two of them agree on a sign that will tell them whether to climb.

The daring attack that follows sets off panic throughout the Philistine camp, and the earth itself shakes. ⟦p:saul_2478|Saul⟧'s watchmen see the enemy scattering, and Israel joins the pursuit. But the victory is clouded by Saul's own command. He has bound his army with a rash oath, forbidding anyone to eat until evening, and ⟦p:jonathan_1692|Jonathan⟧, who did not hear it, tastes some wild honey. The rest of the day turns on that oath and its consequences. The chapter closes with a summary of Saul's wars and family, including his daughters Merab and ⟦p:michal_2073|Michal⟧ and his cousin ⟦p:abner_57|Abner⟧, commander of his army.
15:
⟦p:saul_2478|Saul⟧ has fought on every side, but this chapter brings a single mission that will decide his future. ⟦p:samuel_2469|Samuel⟧ comes to him with a command from the Lord. The Amalekites, a nomadic people of the southern deserts, were the first to attack Israel after the exodus, falling on the weak and weary at the rear of the column. God had promised then that he would one day blot out their memory. Now Saul is to carry out that judgement, and to devote everything to destruction, keeping nothing.

⟦p:saul_2478|Saul⟧ gathers a large army and wins the battle, after warning the Kenites, who showed kindness to Israel in the wilderness, to move away first. But he spares ⟦p:agag_109|Agag⟧, the Amalekite king, and the army keeps the best of the livestock.

Then the word of the Lord comes to ⟦p:samuel_2469|Samuel⟧, with a sentence that grieves him so much that he cries out to the Lord all night: I regret that I have made ⟦p:saul_2478|Saul⟧ king. The confrontation that follows at ⟦l:gilgal_476|Gilgal⟧ is a turning point in the book. Saul's explanations, Samuel's famous reply about obedience and sacrifice, and a torn robe all point to one conclusion. The chapter ends with the two men parting, Samuel to ⟦l:ramah_975|Ramah⟧ and Saul to ⟦l:gibeah_466|Gibeah⟧. Samuel never again goes to see Saul, but he mourns for him.
16:
⟦p:samuel_2469|Samuel⟧ is grieving for ⟦p:saul_2478|Saul⟧, but the Lord tells him it is time to move on. ⟦p:david_994|David⟧ has been anointed at ⟦l:bethlehem_218|Bethlehem⟧ and taken into ⟦p:saul_2478|Saul⟧'s service as a musician. Now the scene shifts to the battlefield. 18:

19:

20:
⟦p:david_994|David⟧ has escaped from ⟦l:naioth_873|Naioth⟧, and he goes in search of ⟦p:jonathan_1692|Jonathan⟧. His question is raw: what have I done, that your father wants to kill me? Jonathan cannot believe it. His father, he says, tells him everything.

21:
⟦p:david_994|David⟧ is now a fugitive, alone and without food or weapons. His first stop is ⟦l:nob_900|Nob⟧, a town just north of ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ where the priests of the Lord now serve. 22:
⟦p:david_994|David⟧ has escaped from ⟦l:gath_442|Gath⟧ by pretending to be mad, and now he takes refuge in the cave of ⟦l:adullam_31|Adullam⟧, in the ⟦l:shephelah_1074|foothills⟧ of ⟦l:judah_1280|Judah⟧, south-west of ⟦l:bethlehem_218|Bethlehem⟧. ⟦p:saul_2478|Saul⟧ broke off his pursuit of ⟦p:david_994|David⟧ to deal with a Philistine raid, but now he is back. ⟦p:saul_2478|Saul⟧ has gone home promising never to harm ⟦p:david_994|David⟧ again, but David does not believe him. 28:

31:
While ⟦p:david_994|David⟧ has been rescuing the captives of ⟦l:ziklag_1259|Ziklag⟧, far to the north the great battle has begun.
